QF.id: AIFM CII Investment Landscape and Types_15

question.text: Mr. Karthik Menon, principal at Narmada Venture Debt Fund (Cat II AIF), pitches venture debt to an LP. Per the chapter, which of the following is the MOST accurate characterisation of venture debt?

answer.text: It is a separate AIF category under SEBI AIF Regulations, distinct from venture capital funds.
It is typically highly collateralised bank-like lending at sub-commercial rates.
It is pure equity capital disguised as debt for tax reasons.

It is specialised lending to start-ups that have raised institutional VC equity, carrying higher interest than commercial loans, typically unsecured, and repaid in about 2-3 years from subsequent equity rounds.

explanation.text: The Logic: The chapter states: 'SEBI (AIF) Regulations do not classify venture debt funds as a separate category but as a part of venture capital funds. Venture debt usually carries a higher rate of interest than normal commercial loans to incorporate the higher risk associated with start-ups and is typically unsecured. It is usually paid back in about 2-3 years by financing the repayment with subsequent rounds of equity financing.' The Trap: (A) False — venture debt is a sub-set of VC funds per SEBI AIF Regs, not separate. (B) Opposite of the truth — venture debt is typically UNSECURED and carries HIGHER rates. (C) Venture debt is genuine debt, not masked equity, though it may include warrants. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C covers venture debt in the Cat I Manager context. Taxation papers (e.g., XIX-D Ch 13) deal with TDS under 194LBB on interest flowing through a VCF/VCF-debt AIF. Manager's Pro-Tip: Structuring a Cat I VCF sleeve for venture debt: track coupon + warrant coverage carefully — the equity kicker is taxed separately from the interest coupon at the investor level under Section 115UB. Warrant conversions straddling fiscal years can trigger unexpected capital-gain reporting for LPs.
